messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Librarian
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mei has worked as a librarian for twenty-two years, and for most of that time, she found a deep sense of peace in the hushed reverence of the stacks. That peace shattered eight months ago, during a vacation with her husband, Kenji, and her younger sister, Lien. They had rented a cabin by a river, and on their third night, a torrential storm rolled in. Mei remembers the drumming of rain on the roof, and then, with a suddenness that felt unnatural, complete silence. It was a heavy, expectant quiet that lasted only a moment before the world was consumed by a roar as a flash flood tore the cabin from its foundations. In the churning, black water, she felt Kenji’s hand and then Lien’s, but the current was too strong. She lost her grip on her sister in the consuming darkness.

Since then, the memory of that night has become an unwelcome resident in her mind. It doesn’t arrive gently; it forces its way in without warning, often triggered by the most innocuous things. The memory itself is a landscape of profound grief, a raw and overwhelming sorrow for her sister that feels as fresh as it did in the moments she realized Lien was gone. This constant threat of re-experiencing the trauma has led Mei to feel perpetually on guard. She scans every room she enters, assessing exits and potential dangers, a habit that leaves her mentally exhausted by the end of each day. At the library, a place once defined by comfort, she now only sits at desks where her back is to a solid wall, unable to tolerate the vulnerability of an open space behind her. This constant state of threat seems to prime her mind for the memory, making it more likely to surface when she is already tense and watchful.

The triggers are everywhere, and her hypervigilance ensures she never misses them. The most potent is a sudden silence. When the low hum of conversation and movement in the library ceases for even a moment, it is no longer peaceful; it is the terrifying precursor to disaster. This quiet immediately activates a profound sense of threat, causing her to scan her surroundings for danger. The silence also acts as a key, unlocking the memory of the moments before the flood, and the overwhelming grief washes over her. Her husband, Kenji, a man she has loved for three decades, has also become a trigger. Simply seeing his face can bring the entire event back, as he is inextricably linked to the loss. Night-time is the worst; waking up in the dark plunges her directly back into the black, churning water.

To cope, Mei has developed a series of strategies that have, over time, constricted her life. When a trigger appears—the library falling quiet, or Kenji walking into the room unexpectedly—she has learned to deliberately dissociate. She will fix her gaze on a point on a bookshelf or a crack in the ceiling and consciously try to blank out, to leave her body until the wave of panic or grief subsides. This avoidance of her internal state has consequences; the memories, never fully processed, seem to return with more force later on. Her avoidance is also external. She no longer takes her morning run, as the feeling of a rapidly beating heart is now indistinguishable from terror. She avoids being in the dark at all costs, sleeping with three nightlights, which has strained her relationship with Kenji, who now often sleeps in the guest room. These very strategies have made her more sensitive; by avoiding darkness so intensely, the rare occasion of a power flicker at work feels catastrophically threatening, reinforcing the trigger’s power.

The cycle has become relentless. Her constant state of threat makes her scan for triggers; finding a trigger brings on the intrusive memory; the memory is so painful she uses maladaptive strategies like blanking out to escape it; and these strategies prevent the memory from ever fading, ensuring it will return. It was Kenji who finally insisted she seek help. He found her standing in the kitchen last week, staring vacantly at the wall, unresponsive for nearly a minute after the kettle had boiled dry with a sudden click into silence. Mei admits she feels trapped. Her world has shrunk to the spaces between her triggers, and she is terrified that she is losing her mind. She came to therapy hoping, more than anything, to one day be able to sit in a quiet room without believing that disaster is about to strike.
